analysis.one_liner: Doubles warning notice before plant closings and mass layoffs and strengthens enforcement.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died when the 111th Congress ended, despite 62 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The Forewarn Act would strengthen the existing WARN Act, which requires employers to warn workers before shutting a plant or conducting a mass layoff. It would extend the required notice from 60 to 90 days, cover smaller employers (75 or more employees instead of 100) and their parent companies, require notices to spell out workers' rights and available benefits, and add Labor Department enforcement — workers could file complaints with the Secretary, who could investigate and sue on their behalf. It also doubles the daily back-pay penalty and bars employers from having workers waive these rights in severance settlements.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at factories and workplaces with 75 or more employees facing a closing or mass layoff. They would get 90 days' warning instead of 60, written notice of their rights and available benefits like unemployment insurance and COBRA health coverage, on-site access to rapid-response reemployment teams, and a Labor Department complaint process with subpoena power. The doubled penalty and the ban on waiving rights in settlements would make the warning requirement harder for employers to buy their way around.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing plant closings and mass layoffs

how_it_helps.text: Extends the required advance notice of a plant closing or mass layoff from 60 to 90 days [S2] [S3].

Covers employers with 75 or more employees instead of 100, counts part-time workers, and pulls in parent corporations, closing loopholes that let large companies lay off workers site by site [S2] [S3].

Requires notices to state each employee's rights to wages, severance, and benefits, and requires employers to tell workers about unemployment compensation, trade adjustment assistance, COBRA benefits, and job training services [S2] [S3].

Lets workers file complaints with the Secretary of Labor, who must investigate, gets subpoena power, and can sue in court to recover back pay, interest, and liquidated damages for employees [S2] [S3].

Doubles the penalty owed to workers — two days' pay per day of missed notice instead of one — and bars any agreement or settlement from waiving these rights except ones negotiated by the Secretary, a state attorney general, or the employees' own attorney [S2] [S3].
Requires employers to let federal, state, and local rapid-response reemployment teams meet with affected workers on site, during work hours [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 75 or more employees who close plants or conduct mass layoffs — especially manufacturers and other businesses that restructure. They would owe an extra month of wages to workers laid off with less than 90 days' notice, provide more detailed notices, post the law at their workplaces, and face federal enforcement including lawsuits by the Labor Department. Businesses argued the longer notice period and doubled liability raise the cost of restructuring, though the bill exempts closings caused directly by a terrorist attack and lets courts reduce liability where employers made good-faith efforts to comply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers of 75+ that close plants or lay off workers

drawbacks.text: The doubled penalty — two days' pay per day of shortfall — and the ban on waiver could push employers toward settlements that shift restructuring costs, and small-to-midsize firms newly covered at the 75-employee threshold would face compliance costs they did not have before [S2] [S3].

The 90-day notice requirement is hard to meet when closings happen suddenly for financial reasons; even under the existing 60-day WARN Act, employers in sudden distress often cannot give full notice, and a longer requirement could mean more violations rather than more actual warning.
The bill authorizes appropriations for additional Labor Department enforcement without specifying an amount, leaving the enforcement machinery's funding to the appropriations process [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give workers facing job loss a month of additional warning, clearer information about benefits, and a real federal complaint process instead of having to hire a lawyer to sue. The main cost falls on employers that close facilities, in the form of an extra month of wages when notice falls short and a doubled penalty. The strongest objection is that a 90-day notice period can be impossible for a company in sudden financial distress, which could turn the law into a source of litigation rather than warning. On balance, the provisions would meaningfully strengthen a warning law that workers often could not enforce on their own.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup or a floor vote, dying when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller (D-CA) introduced the Forewarn Act on June 25, 2009, with Reps. McHugh (R-NY), Woolsey (D-CA), and Kaptur (D-OH) as original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day of introduction; that is the only action recorded before the Congress ended [S5].
The bill attracted 62 cosponsors, including 61 of 253 House Democrats and 1 of 178 House Republicans, but the committee never took it up [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that close plants or conduct mass layoffs are better off: they continue to operate under the weaker 60-day, 100-employee WARN Act rules, with no added Labor Department enforcement and no doubled penalty. Workers get nothing from this bill, and companies needing to restructure also avoid the longer notice obligation it would have imposed.

industries.industry: Large employers (75+ employees) that close plants or conduct mass layoffs, especially manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have cost these employers an extra month of wages when notice falls short, a doubled daily penalty, and new federal enforcement. Their interest in avoiding these obligations runs directly against workers' interest in advance warning, and the bill's failure leaves the weaker status quo in place.

industries.industry: Labor Department and state rapid-response workforce agencies
industries.note: The bill would have given the Labor Department complaint intake, subpoena power, and litigation authority, and required employers to give rapid-response teams on-site access to affected workers, expanding their role in helping laid-off workers find new jobs.
